Our approach

A place to begin.
A way to go deeper.

This atlas turns a starting list of 454 names into an accessible research directory. It preserves the original entries, adds supported omissions, and places sources alongside the reading.

What is here so far

469 entries · 15 additions · 8 collections with 12+ inspected sources · 30 expanded profiles · 35 brief cited overviews · 404 source guides · 1222 unique resources

Every original entry has its own accessible page. The depth varies, and the site labels that difference. An expanded profile develops several themes with section citations, a recorded source-review date, and explicit gaps. A cited overview is a shorter introduction drawn from identified sources. A source guide is a shorter orientation with annotated reading. The research minimum is at least 12 excellent, directly relevant sources for each tribe or nation, with more where useful. Duplicate mirrors, bare homepages, passing mentions, and unread bibliographies do not fill that minimum. Existing expanded profiles will be deepened toward the same standard. A recorded content check can cover identified sections or an available excerpt; annotations state such limits. Source quantity and these editorial labels do not mean that a comprehensive, community-reviewed deep dive is complete. Browse the expanded profiles.

The intended next stage is a fuller researched article for each entry: identity and names; homelands and historical change; language and cultural life; governance and contemporary community priorities; and a bibliography with community voices at its center. Gaps in this collection are research tasks, not evidence that a people has no contemporary presence.

Names need context

The starting list mixes peoples, political nations, individual communities, language groupings, and historical names. It also includes overlapping names. These are kept as separate access points so readers can find the name they know; naming notes and related entries explain relationships where the sources support them.

For example, a broad entry such as Pueblo is a route into multiple distinct communities. A term such as Ohlone also covers distinct communities and identities. Some entries use an outside name, while others use a community’s own name. A cross-link alone never establishes that two communities are interchangeable.

Search ignores accents and common apostrophe differences to make names easier to find, while displayed names retain their spelling. Preferred and alternate names are included where research established them. The atlas does not determine citizenship, identity, or recognition.

Begin with Indigenous voices

Profiles prioritize sources published by the people or nation concerned, community cultural organizations, language programs, and Indigenous representative bodies. Sources are labeled by origin or format and annotated for relevance. Reporting and public interviews are identified separately; annotations distinguish an author’s own account from an institution’s policy. Government, university, museum, and archival resources add context, but do not replace community perspectives.

The Smithsonian’s Native Knowledge 360° framework, developed with Native communities, offers useful guidance for understanding diverse and continuing Indigenous lives. It informs this directory’s emphasis on specific communities and contemporary context.

How the research develops

Each entry moves through source discovery, reading and relevance checks, synthesis with section citations, and editorial review. We prioritize the relevant nation’s own publications, identify the scope and date of outside accounts, and distinguish a proposed project from a completed result. A working URL alone does not establish that a source supports a claim.

Expanded profiles record unresolved questions instead of filling gaps with assumptions. When dates conflict, the text attributes the disagreement or uses a supported date range. Language endangerment is not evidence that a people has disappeared. Umbrella names, individual governments, historical towns, and related languages require separate treatment.

The current priority is to deepen every A entry before returning to further B research. 4 of 27 A collections currently contain at least 12 inspected substantive resources. The remaining A entries require the same careful reading, fuller articles, and evidence review. The first four have now been revisited; reaching the source minimum leaves their stated gaps and community review open. Browse all A entries. Quality depends on relevant, traceable evidence and breadth of perspectives. Reaching the numerical minimum is one milestone in that work. Browse collections with 12 or more inspected sources, or view the progress record.

Scope and completeness

The directory follows the starting list across what are now Canada, the United States, Mexico, and Central America, with additional entries where verified sources support them. Modern country lines do not define the limits of Indigenous homelands. Regional labels are broad finding aids, and are not territorial boundaries.

This is an expanding collection, not an exhaustive list. The number of entries must not be read as the number of distinct Indigenous nations. Administrative lists also have specific limits: the U.S. Tribal Leaders Directory, Canada’s First Nation Profiles, and Mexico’s INPI atlas organize information for different purposes.

How to read a profile

  1. Read the identity and naming notes, including relationships to other entries.
  2. Use the cited sections for orientation. Section citations jump to the supporting source cards.
  3. Start with Indigenous-led sources where available. The annotations explain what each resource contributes.
  4. Follow related communities and compare sources’ dates, scope, and authorship.
  5. Save entries to your browser’s reading list, or print a profile with its source URLs.

Editorial limits and maintenance

The material was compiled on October 19, 2026. It is an independent research collection and has not been reviewed or endorsed by the listed communities. Links can change, and legal status, officeholders, population estimates, and community initiatives require checking against current community sources.

Only publicly available sources are linked. A public reference is not permission to reproduce or interpret restricted cultural knowledge. Short summaries and annotations lead readers to the publishers’ original work.

The downloadable research data keeps the profile text, source metadata, original-list identifiers, research labels, and relationship notes together. It can support continued research and corrections without losing the evidence behind an entry.

Many nations. Many histories.
Follow the sources. Listen to the people.
